defects.opened: 2026-08-03 sess69 (ccloop c7ee71c6) — audit of GPT sess68 refusal item 4; ledgered sess70
defects.summary: mxfs_disklock_purge_node() published its zeroing of a dead node's lock records and heartbeat sector with a plain read-modify-write, with no interlock against the other survivors running the identical purge for the same victim — a delayed second purge could zero a slot a LIVE node had since claimed, destroying its grant, or erase a live node's heartbeat record and cause the cluster to fence and replay a node that was still writing
defects.found: Code path, line-proven.  SHIPPED in every build with the disklock purge.  Fixed in 0.11.412; the concurrent-purger race itself is not yet exercised by any test.
evidence: Both zeroing sites in mxfs_disklock_purge_node() did read_sector() then write_sector() — a read-modify-write with no compare-and-write and no lock that spans nodes.
There are SIX call sites, and dlm/mount.c:1057 and dlm/mount.c:1126 run one on EVERY survivor at peer death, so concurrent purgers are the normal case at 32 nodes, not an exotic timing.

Losing interleaving, no exotic timing required: P1 reads slot S (the dead node's ACTIVE grant); P2 reads slot S (same image); P2 writes zero (S is free); live node E claims S and writes its own ACTIVE grant; P1 writes zero — E's LIVE grant is destroyed.  E then believes it holds a lock that no longer exists on disk, so the same resource can be granted twice.

The heartbeat variant is worse: the late zero erases a LIVE node's heartbeat record, every peer declares that node dead, and the cluster fences it and replays its journal slice while it is still writing to the LUN — split brain.

A SECOND, INDEPENDENT hole in the same function, found during the same audit: the sess65 phase-0 freeze gate was evaluated on a read taken BEFORE the 65536-record scan, but the zero pass re-checked only recov_desc_names() ('does the descriptor name this victim') — not its stage, not its owner, and not the unreadable/torn case.  A descriptor that advanced, changed owner, or became torn during the scan was published anyway, defeating the freeze gate entirely.
defects.why_it_was_not_caught: The purge reads as a cleanup step rather than a publication, and cleanup of a node everyone agrees is dead looks idempotent — zeroing an already-zero sector is a no-op.  What makes it not idempotent is slot REUSE: the sector's meaning changes when a live node claims the slot, and the second purger is still holding an image from before that happened.  No test creates a slot-reuse window inside a concurrent purge.
fix: FIXED in 0.11.412 (dlm/disklock.c), verification still owed.

purge_cas_zero() — publication is now mxfs_pal_bdev_compare_and_write() of the exact validated image.  -EAGAIN (MISCOMPARE) causes a re-read and re-derivation of the decision, bounded by MXFS_PURGE_CAS_RETRIES (4); exhausting the retries is counted as incompleteness, never as success.

purge_hb_zeroable() — the full freeze gate (quarantine / stage / owner+epoch / torn) is re-derived on the image the CAS publishes against, using recov_lease_covers() so a torn descriptor returns -EPROTO instead of being silently skipped.  Gate and publish are now one atomic step.

-EOPNOTSUPP fallback is reachable only when mxfs_bdev_to_sdev() finds no SCSI device behind the bdev — i.e. not a shared LUN, so no second purger can exist.  It falls back to a plain write and COUNTS it as P235-PURGE-NONATOMIC; never silently.
New probes P235-PURGE-CONTENDED, P235-PURGE-CONTENDED-HB, P235-PURGE-REFROZE feed the existing sess59 honesty accounting, so an incomplete purge still returns < 0 and recovery is NOT published.
defects.why_still_open: RULE 6: the fix is landed and the board proves it did not break the normal single-death path (0.11.412 boarded green: fence_during_write 32/32 8/8 checks 17s/60s, crash_consistency 32/32 204/204 checks 86s/90s, dir_reuse_coherency 32/32 93/93 checks 107s/120s), but the board does NOT exercise the concurrent-purger race that motivated the change.  A clean run on the path that was already working is not a disposition.
defects.next: 1) Build a test that forces two survivors to purge the SAME victim concurrently and asserts no live slot is zeroed — the CAS MISCOMPARE probes (P235-PURGE-CONTENDED / -HB) are the observable, so the test can assert the interlock actually fired rather than merely that nothing broke.  2) Include the torn/advancing-descriptor arm: force a descriptor stage advance during the 65536-record scan and assert P235-PURGE-REFROZE.  3) Only then FIXED AND VERIFIED.

defects.opened: sess77 (GPT RULE-5 ruling); root proven on the rig sess78
defects.found: 0.11.416 and every prior version that had a recovery guard
defects.summary: The disklock heartbeat wrote its own slot sector with an UNCONDITIONAL blind write. Any state a survivor had stamped into that sector while the node was being recovered -- specifically a RECOVERY_GUARD record, which is the one-shot certificate that a fence happened and a journal-slice replay is in progress -- was overwritten by the victim's next heartbeat, ~1.8s later. Two consequences: (a) the fence certificate is destroyed, so a survivor cannot prove it fenced the node, and (b) the node being recovered re-advertises itself as live in the middle of its own journal replay.
defects.mechanism: dlm/disklock.c heartbeat path issued a plain bdev write to slot_off(local_slot) with no compare. Three further sites wrote the same sector blind: the heartbeat (site 1), release_slot (site 2), and the withdraw stamp (site 3). Because the guard lives IN the victim's own slot sector (there is nowhere else that both parties agree on), 'my own slot' is not the same as 'a sector only I may write'.
defects.evidence: MEASURED on the 32-node CAW rig, sess78, tests/hb_guard_clobber_probe.sh: against 0.11.416 a survivor-stamped RECOVERY_GUARD in test2's slot 25 was destroyed at t+0.8s by test2's next heartbeat and test2 logged NOTHING -- it did not notice, did not stop, did not self-fence. Probe verdict line: guard gone, flags reverted to live-heartbeat.
defects.fix: 0.11.417/0.11.418: the heartbeat write became a compare-and-write against a cached image of our own last-written record (ctx->hb_img / hb_img_valid, dlm/disklock.c:~500-580). On CAS miscompare the sector is re-read and classified: (a) still our live record -> P236-HB-CAS-RESYNC, re-sync the compare image and retry (a drifted cache, not a takeover); (b) anything else -> P236-HB-FOREIGN-WRITE + -EPERM, which drives a SELF-FENCE. Sites 2 and 3 became refusals: P236-RELEASE-REFUSED (disklock.c:1337) and P236-WITHDRAW-REFUSED (disklock.c:2021) both decline to overwrite a foreign/guard record rather than destroying it.
defects.verification: RULE 4 loop closed on the rig, sess79, on BOTH 0.11.417 and 0.11.418. tests/hb_guard_clobber_probe.sh test2 test1 -- full PASS condition (HELD alone would NOT have been sufficient; all four lines required): 'VERDICT: HELD for 12s -- flags stayed RECOVERY_GUARD'; 'P236-HB-FOREIGN-WRITE slot=25 ... own-slot CAS MISCOMPARE'; 'P236-SELF-FENCE ... stopping heartbeat, forcing shutdown'; 'P236-WITHDRAW-REFUSED slot=25 ... would destroy it'. So the guard now survives, the victim NOTICES (it did not before), and the withdraw path refuses to stamp over it. No P-HB-SLOW regression under the new build (zero on the fixed build; test1's two predate the deploy and are write_ms=0 with multi-second lockwait_ms -- lock wait, not the CAS).
defects.residual_note: Two limits, both tracked elsewhere and NEITHER a gap in this fix: (1) call site 2 (release_slot) is not exercised by this probe -- it needs an unmount with a guard present; the refusal is code-verified but not rig-verified. (2) Detection latency is ~1.8s (one heartbeat interval): the victim stops itself one HB after the guard is stamped, so a survivor that assumes the fence takes effect instantly is still wrong. That is D-VICTIM-REPLAY-WITHOUT-PROVEN-EXCLUSION, which remains OPEN.
defects.updated: sess80 (entry created; sess78 shipped the fix without a ledger entry)

defects.found: 0.11.417 and every prior version since the sess131 self-fence message was written
defects.summary: MXFS's most severe operator message told admins their shared LUN had been destroyed when it had not. Four distinct detectors fire a self-fence; all four printed 'P131-SELF-FENCE: device reformatted under live mount'. Only ONE of the four is that condition. The other three -- own-slot takeover, PR key lost while fencing, PR key preempted -- are ordinary cluster fencing on an intact device, and they provoked a data-loss panic response from the operator instead of a fencing response.
defects.mechanism: Neither fence callback typedef carried a reason: mxfs_disklock_fence_cb and mxfs_v5_fence_notify_fn both took only the mount context, so the XFS layer at xfs/xfs_mxfs_dlm.c had no way to know WHY it was being fenced and hardcoded the only cause that existed when the message was written. Worse, the two SCSI-PR paths (dlm/v5_mount.c:739 and :991) never went through the disklock log at all -- they call fence_notify_fn directly, so they emitted ONLY the false XFS line with no truthful line anywhere.
defects.evidence: Source-proven, then rig-confirmed. Before: every self-fence, whatever its trigger, printed the reformat text. The sess78 guard probe fires the SLOT_TAKEOVER detector specifically, and on 0.11.417 it printed 'device reformatted under live mount' -- a false statement about the operator's data, produced by the fencing path working correctly.
defects.fix: 0.11.418: added enum mxfs_self_fence_reason to include/mxfs/mxfs_common.h:115 with mxfs_self_fence_reason_name() and _desc() kept immediately beside it, so a new detector cannot be added without also writing the operator explanation. Four reasons: FS_IDENTITY (disklock, genuinely re-mkfs'd -- the only one the old text was right about), SLOT_TAKEOVER (disklock, own-slot CAS miscompare), PR_KEY_LOST_FENCING (v5_mount.c:739), PR_KEY_PREEMPTED (v5_mount.c:991). Both typedefs now take int reason; the XFS emitter (xfs/xfs_mxfs_dlm.c:42041) prints the reason name and its description instead of a constant, and v5_mount.c:1223 now logs a truthful P131 line on the PR paths that previously logged none.
defects.verification: Rig-verified sess79 on 0.11.418: the SLOT_TAKEOVER path now prints 'P131-SELF-FENCE [SLOT_TAKEOVER]: a surviving peer declared this node dead and is replaying its journal slice -- this mount has been fenced by the cluster, the device is intact'. The claim about the device is now true, and it names the actual detector. Build: clean.
defects.residual_note: FS_IDENTITY, PR_KEY_LOST_FENCING and PR_KEY_PREEMPTED are code-verified (each detector passes its own constant) but not individually rig-triggered. The defect was that the reason was not plumbed at all; the plumbing is single-valued per call site and the enum is exhaustively switched, so a wrong reason would be a compile-visible mismatch, not a runtime one.

defects.found: every version since P49-STALEBASE was added
defects.summary: The P49-STALEBASE probe printed garbage in its own summary clause. The format string had 16 conversion specifiers and 15 arguments: the trailing prose 'missing %d durable peer dirent(s)' had no argument, so vsnprintf read an uninitialised va_arg slot. This is an evidence-integrity defect -- a probe whose output cannot be trusted is worse than no probe, because it is read as data.
defects.mechanism: xfs/libxfs/xfs_dir2_data.c:1712, the P49-STALEBASE pr_warn_ratelimited. The count was already carried by the machine-readable field missing=%d earlier in the same line; the human-readable tail repeated the specifier without repeating the argument.
defects.evidence: Compiler-proven: a FULL rebuild emits -Wformat for this call site. Method trap worth recording -- the warning only surfaces on a full rebuild (an incremental build with an untouched object file emits nothing), and filtering the build log with grep -iE 'error|warning' HIDES which file it came from, because the file name appears on the 'note: in expansion of macro' lines, not on the warning line. Capture the whole build log and grep with context.
defects.fix: 0.11.418: the tail no longer takes a specifier -- it reads 'in-core base missing the durable peer dirent(s) listed above; whole-block writeback will clobber them'. Specifier and argument counts now match.
defects.verification: Full rebuild of the whole tree after the fix: -Wformat warning count = 0. The compiler is the complete oracle for this defect class -- it checks every call site, not just the one observed. Tree-wide audit done at the same time: mxfs_pal_log IS __printf(2,3)-annotated (pal/pal.h:566-571), so the entire dlm/ layer was already format-checked, and this was the ONLY mismatch in the tree.

defects.summary: The pass-1 'own-stamp reclaim' slot claim - which xfs_log.c:623 calls 'the required own-crash recovery path' and which is the ONLY path that keeps slice_adopted=false (full replay of a node's own previous incarnation) - can never match, because the node_id it matches on is a fresh random value at every mount. Every mount is therefore a pass-2 fresh claim that sets XLOG_MXFS_ADOPTED_SLICE and suppresses image replay of the inherited slice.
defects.evidence: sess89 fleet measurement on 32/caw at 0.11.420 (srcversion 33018595D555FBE463F017B): 91 'claimed heartbeat slot' lines across all 32 nodes' full dmesg history - 0 'own-stamp reclaim', 91 'fresh claim - slice ADOPTED'. Successive mounts of the SAME host carry unrelated node ids (test1: 1401183219 -> 2204047808 -> 2583145845), and nodes migrate slots freely across mounts (test30: 30 -> 2 -> 1). Root is line-verified: v5_mount.c:2494 mxfs_pal_get_random_bytes(node_uuid,16) on every mxfs_v5_dlm_init, node_id = uuid_to_node_id(node_uuid) (v5_mount.c:375,2497), and there is no persistence of node_uuid anywhere in the tree. disklock.c:4619 pass-1 matches expected->node_id == ctx->local_node.
defects.mechanism: disklock.c:4578-4584 states the invariant the code relies on: pass-1 'is what lets a rebooted node re-claim its own slot with slice_adopted=false, i.e. FULL replay of its PREVIOUS incarnation's log records', and warns that pushing a rebooted node onto pass-2 means 'silently abandoning that node's own unreplayed journal slice'. That warned-of state is the UNCONDITIONAL behaviour. Two shipped consequences: (1) the own-crash replay path never runs - every node depends entirely on a SURVIVOR's peer-death recovery to replay its slice, so the whole-cluster-crash / no-survivor case has no proven replayer; (2) MXFS_RECOVERY_SUPERSEDED (disklock.h, disklock.c:2824-2839) is unreachable dead code, since its precondition is a same-node-id later incarnation on the slot.
defects.containment: Not a live corruption on the measured paths. sess89 probed the adjacent hazard - pass-2 stealing a WITHDRAWN slot that still owes replay - and REFUTED it by measurement: the RECOVERY_GUARD lands 1.26s after the WITHDRAWN stamp (O_DIRECT timeline, ACTIVE t+0.00 -> WITHDRAWN t+2.06 -> GUARD t+3.32 -> zeroed t+11.37), a remount needs ~12s, and pass-2 skips GUARD slots, so the remount correctly took free slot 32 and 100/100 fsync-acknowledged files survived. The exposure that remains unmeasured is the case with NO survivor to run the peer-death recovery.
defects.next: 1) RULE-5 consult: is a stable per-node identity the right fix (persisted node_uuid / identity derived from the slot+incarnation pair), or should pass-1 be deleted and the adopted-slice gate made the single documented path with the no-survivor case covered explicitly? Two plausible shapes - do not pick one unaided. 2) Measure the no-survivor case directly: crash ALL 32 nodes with fsync-acknowledged payload outstanding, bring one back, and assert the payload survives - this is the one path with no proven replayer. 3) Whatever the fix, either make SUPERSEDED reachable and exercise it on the rig, or delete it - a shipped safety arm that cannot execute is not evidence of anything. 4) tests/withdraw_slot_reclaim_probe.sh is the persistent instrument for the claim/guard race; it prints the O_DIRECT slot timeline and the claim kind.

defects.summary: A durable recovery descriptor whose victim_epoch is 0 can NEVER be advanced by its own owner, so the recovery is replayed but never published: GRANTS_RELEASED is never reached, purge_node's freeze gate refuses to zero the sector, the dead node's CAW authority bits stay held forever, and the owner retries the advance in an unbounded silent loop.  recovery_begin CREATES such descriptors by design (the P237-RECOV-INC-UNOBSERVED arm, for callers that never observed the victim's incarnation), so creation and authentication contradict each other.
defects.evidence: MEASURED sess91 on the live 32-node CAW rig, build 0.11.420 srcversion 33018595D555FBE463F017B, via tests/incarnation_mismatch_probe.sh arm=zero.  Sequence: kill test32 (slot 4, node 4085327405, incarnation 1634619062121349274); rewrite ONLY the 8-byte epoch field of its now-unwritten HB sector to 0 with a recomputed feature CRC (512B O_DIRECT from test1).  Round 1 refused correctly (see D-MOUNT-INCARNATION-CONSTANT-ZERO).  Round 2: 'P237-RECOV-INC-UNOBSERVED slot=4 victim=4085327405 on-disk=0' then 'P234-RECOV-FENCED slot=4 victim=4085327405 epoch=0 slice=0/4 owner=4195151743 gen=1 term=1'.  The slice REPLAYED ('MXFS: foreign replay of slot 4 complete' x10, 'P163-RECOVERED slot=4' x31).  Every advance then failed: 'P234-RECOV-NOTOURS slot=4 victim=4085327405 stage->3 — the descriptor is owned by node=4195151743 epoch=14541807080602951442 gen=1 term=1; we hold node=4195151743 epoch=14541807080602951442 gen=1 term=1.  We were taken over while we worked' — THE TWO TUPLES PRINTED ARE IDENTICAL — and 'P234-COMPLETE-REPLAYEDFAIL slot=4 node=4085327405 rc=-16' (-EBUSY) x7.  12 minutes after the kill the sector still read flags=RECOVERY_GUARD(3) stage=2(FENCED) victim_epoch=0 owner_epoch=14541807080602951442, the owner had logged 11 NOTOURS retries and counting, P163-RECOVERY-COMPLETE=0 and P97-SWEEP-DONE=0 cluster-wide.
defects.mechanism: dlm/disklock.c: inc_eq(a,b) is 'a != 0 && b != 0 && a == b' — the deliberate 'zero is never a wildcard' comparator for CROSS-SOURCE incarnation matching (sess83 RULE-5 ruling).  recov_auth_holds() (disklock.c:2722) uses it for a SELF-CONSISTENCY test instead: 'inc_eq(d->victim_epoch, auth->victim_epoch)', where auth was issued verbatim from that same descriptor by recov_auth_issue() (auth->victim_epoch = d->victim_epoch, 0 included).  inc_eq(0,0) is false by construction, so the owner fails its own authentication and mxfs_disklock_recovery_advance() returns -EBUSY at disklock.c:2985 forever.  The identical shape is at disklock.c:3291 (the fencing-lease auth).  Downstream: v5_mount.c:2257 P234-COMPLETE-REPLAYEDFAIL returns rc without bounding the retry, and mxfs_disklock_purge_node's freeze gate refuses to zero a sector below GRANTS_RELEASED, so the slot and the dead node's grants are permanently frozen.
defects.containment: None.  The retry loop is silent apart from the misleading NOTOURS text, which asserts a takeover that did not happen and names two identical tuples as evidence of it.
defects.next: CLOSED sess91.  Successor work is on D-RECOV-ADVANCE-UNBOUNDED-RETRY (bounded retry/classify/relinquish/escalate, plus the provenance audit of the ~6 remaining inc_eq(d->victim_epoch, victim_epoch) sites and the slot-quarantine invariants for a zero-victim_epoch descriptor) and D-MONITOR-INCARNATION-DOWNGRADE-TO-ZERO.
defects.found: sess91
defects.disposition: FIXED AND VERIFIED sess91, same session it was found.  CAUSE (RULE 4, proven not guessed): the P234-RECOV-NOTOURS line printed two IDENTICAL owner tuples as its evidence of a takeover, which located the failure in the token half of recov_auth_holds(); inc_eq(0,0) is false by construction and auth->victim_epoch is copied verbatim from d->victim_epoch, so the owner could not authenticate against its own descriptor.  PATCH (0.11.421, dlm/disklock.c): a second, deliberately differently named comparator recov_tok_eq() for DESCRIPTOR-TOKEN identity (exact encoded equality, so UNKNOWN equals the UNKNOWN it was issued from) alongside inc_eq() for CROSS-SOURCE incarnation proof (zero always fails); both recov_auth_holds() and recov_fence_auth_holds() switched to it for victim_epoch, and both additionally now compare victim_slot — which recov_auth_issue()/recov_fence_auth_issue() have always copied and nothing ever checked, so a stale auth could pass against a different slot's descriptor (not zero-specific; it applied to nonzero incarnations too).  The NOTOURS diagnostic now names which test failed (TAKEOVER vs TOKEN-MISMATCH) and prints both full tuples, so it can never again assert a takeover it did not observe.  VERIFICATION: the IDENTICAL injection (tests/incarnation_mismatch_probe.sh arm=zero) re-run on the fixed build, A/B on the same rig — P234-RECOV-NOTOURS 7 -> 0, P234-COMPLETE-REPLAYEDFAIL 7 -> 0, P163-RECOVERY-COMPLETE 0 -> 1, P97-SWEEP-DONE 0 -> 1, and the slot went from RECOVERY_GUARD/stage=2 still frozen after 12 minutes and 11 retries, to ZEROED at t+30s.  The refusal arm is unchanged (P237-RECOV-INC-MISMATCH 3 -> 3, P234-COMPLETE-FENCEFAIL 3 -> 3), so the fix did not weaken the guard it runs behind.  Regression gate: full 32/caw board on 0.11.421 — 27 of 27 functional criteria PASS.  PRODUCTION REACHABILITY, measured not assumed: a zero victim_epoch descriptor is what the P237-RECOV-INC-UNOBSERVED arm creates, and it has two producers — the lease detector (v5_mount.c:1405-1432 passes dead_slot=-1, dead_epoch=0 by design) and the monitor's own downgrade of a known incarnation to 0.  A fleet-wide search of every retained dmesg and journalctl -k found ZERO 'lease expired/died' lines with slot -1, so on this rig the lease arm has never fired: the disklock monitor declares dead at 62s + confirm while the lease timeout is pinned at 600s (lease.c:333).  So this wedge was NOT routine on a healthy default deployment.  It WAS, however, a genuine shipped defect on a real path and not merely an artifact of the injection: any node death the disk monitor cannot witness within 600s, and any death whose slot sector reads a zero incarnation, produces the descriptor that 0.11.420 could never advance — replay completes, then the recovery hangs at FENCED for ever with the dead node's CAW grants frozen.  The injection made that path reproducible on demand.  THE WEDGE ONLY: the further items the sess91 RULE-5 ruling raised are NOT covered here and are filed as their own OPEN entries — D-RECOV-ADVANCE-UNBOUNDED-RETRY and D-MONITOR-INCARNATION-DOWNGRADE-TO-ZERO.

defects.summary: A recovery milestone that cannot be advanced BY AN OWNER THAT STILL PASSES THE OWNERSHIP TEST is retried for ever, silently, with the victim's grants frozen behind it — no bound, no backoff, no classification, no relinquish, no escalation.
defects.evidence: MEASURED sess91 on the live 32-node rig at 0.11.420, as the containment failure behind D-RECOV-AUTH-ZERO-VICTIM-EPOCH-WEDGE.  With recovery_advance permanently returning -EBUSY, the elected owner logged 11 P234-RECOV-NOTOURS / P234-COMPLETE-REPLAYEDFAIL pairs over 12 minutes with no change in behaviour, no rate limiting, no escalation and no takeover; the on-disk sector held flags=RECOVERY_GUARD stage=2(FENCED) throughout, P163-RECOVERY-COMPLETE and P97-SWEEP-DONE stayed at 0 cluster-wide, and the slot was never reclaimed.  The specific -EBUSY source is fixed in 0.11.421, but the retry structure that turned it into an indefinite hang is unchanged: any other permanent advance failure (a genuine takeover the old owner keeps retrying, a persistent I/O error on the sector, a QUARANTINED descriptor) reproduces the identical loop.  SCOPE NARROWED sess91 by a second measurement, and the original wording was too broad.  tests/recov_takeover_retry_probe.sh made an advance fail permanently in the OTHER way — a genuine takeover, where the owner check itself fails — and the owner did NOT loop: it logged exactly ONE P234-RECOV-NOTOURS (kind=TAKEOVER) over 133s and stopped, because recovery_begin's re-entry also fails the ownership test and returns -EBUSY with P234-RECOV-OWNED instead of re-attempting the completion.  So the unbounded loop requires the owner to keep PASSING recov_auth_holds' owner test while FAILING something downstream — exactly the shape of the fixed wedge.  That does not make the defect benign: nothing bounds it when it does occur, and the takeover-class failure instead deadlocks permanently (D-RECOVERY-TAKEOVER-UNREACHABLE).  The same run positively VERIFIED the 0.11.421 P234-RECOV-NOTOURS rework, which had shipped observed only in its not-firing state: kind=TAKEOVER fired correctly with both full tuples printed and zero spurious kind=TOKEN-MISMATCH.
defects.mechanism: dlm/v5_mount.c: every failure arm of the completion path (P234-COMPLETE-FENCEFAIL, P234-COMPLETE-REPLAYEDFAIL, P234-COMPLETE-RELEASEDFAIL, P230-COMPLETE-CAWFAIL, P230-COMPLETE-FLUSHFAIL, P230-COMPLETE-PURGEFAIL) returns rc with the comment 'the pending marker and heartbeat record stay set for a retry' and no attempt counter, deadline, backoff or escalation.  mxfs_disklock_purge_node's freeze gate correctly refuses to zero a sector below GRANTS_RELEASED, so the dead node's CAW authority bits stay held for as long as the loop runs — which is forever.
defects.containment: None.  The loop is quiet: an ERR-level line per attempt with no counter, no 'attempt N of M', and (before 0.11.421) misleading text.
defects.next: Per the sess91 RULE-5 ruling: (1) On each failure REREAD the descriptor and CLASSIFY.  If owner/gen/term/recovery-id genuinely changed, stop immediately, discard the auth and let the new owner continue — do not keep retrying. (2) If the descriptor is unchanged and still ours yet auth fails, that is an INVARIANT VIOLATION, not contention: emit a fatal diagnostic naming every compared field and STOP the loop.  Do not force the milestone and do not clear the guard. (3) For transient storage errors use bounded retries with backoff and a deadline; past the deadline, relinquish recovery ownership so a takeover can occur, and if that is not possible escalate the filesystem to degraded/read-only/failed.  Safety forbids skipping GRANTS_RELEASED or purging uncertain authority to preserve availability; liveness forbids the unbounded quiet loop.  The eventual safe outcome may be service failure rather than successful recovery — but it must be a terminating, loud one. (4) Add the owner-incarnation NEGATIVE arm carried over from D-MOUNT-INCARNATION-CONSTANT-ZERO: inject a same-node LATER incarnation attempting to advance a predecessor's descriptor (the 'A -> B -> A within a single session' case, disklock.h:261) and assert inc_eq(d->owner_epoch, ctx->epoch) refuses it and the new classification reports TAKEOVER, not TOKEN-MISMATCH.
defects.found: sess91

defects.summary: The heartbeat monitor overwrites a KNOWN nonzero cached victim incarnation with 0 when the sector reads 0, treating 'unknown' as an observation.  That is information loss, not an update: it launders an incarnation MISMATCH into the 'never observed' arm, so the next death round publishes a recovery that cannot name which incarnation it is recovering.
defects.evidence: MEASURED sess91 on the live 32-node rig.  With nt->last_epoch holding the victim's real incarnation 1634619062121349274, a sector whose epoch read 0 drove the epoch-change arm to rebase nt->last_epoch to 0 (disklock.c:1156 rebase_epoch, applied at :1358).  Round 1 correctly refused: 'P237-RECOV-INC-MISMATCH ... victim_inc=1634619062121349274 slot_inc=0 ... refusing to publish'.  Round 2, with the cached value now destroyed, took the opposite branch on the SAME facts: 'P237-RECOV-INC-UNOBSERVED slot=4 victim=4085327405 on-disk=0 — the caller never observed the victim's incarnation' and published 'P234-RECOV-FENCED ... epoch=0'.  The caller HAD observed it, 62 seconds earlier, and said so in the log.
defects.mechanism: dlm/disklock.c:1147 fires the epoch-change arm on any difference including a transition to 0; :1156 sets rebase_epoch = rhb->epoch unconditionally and :1358 commits it into nt->last_epoch.  There is no inc_valid() test on the incoming value, so 'known E1' + 'observed UNKNOWN' resolves to UNKNOWN instead of retaining E1 and flagging the sector as inconsistent.  A transition E1 -> E2 (both nonzero) may establish supersession under the sess86 rules; a transition E1 -> 0 cannot establish anything.  Related: the P237-RECOV-INC-UNOBSERVED text calls the sector 'the authority for which incarnation last owned this slice' — the sector is authoritative for SLOT state, but 0 is not an authoritative incarnation under inc_valid(); it is an authoritative statement that the incarnation is unavailable.
defects.containment: None.  Both branches log correctly and neither reports the downgrade, so the contradiction is only visible by reading the two rounds together.
defects.next: Per the sess91 RULE-5 ruling: (1) Guard the rebase with inc_valid(): a nonzero cached incarnation must be RETAINED when the sector reads 0, and the slot marked inconsistent/unknown rather than silently re-baselined.  Decide explicitly what a live-looking ACTIVE record with a zero incarnation means at this proto_gen — no member at gen 3 writes one, so it is either a torn/spliced sector or a foreign writer, and both deserve a distinct probe rather than adoption. (2) Reword P237-RECOV-INC-UNOBSERVED so it does not call 0 an authoritative incarnation. (3) Regression: replay tests/incarnation_mismatch_probe.sh arm=zero and assert round 2 does NOT reach the UNOBSERVED arm once the downgrade is blocked — the correct outcome is a persistent, loud refusal or an explicit slot-quarantine transition, never a recovery published under an unknown incarnation.  Coordinate with D-RECOV-ZERO-EPOCH-DESCRIPTOR-AUTHORITY-UNPROVEN: that entry decides whether a zero-victim_epoch descriptor may exist at all, and this one removes the largest source of them.
defects.found: sess91

defects.summary: recovery_begin publishes recovery descriptors whose victim_epoch is 0 — a deliberate, documented arm — but nothing establishes the slot/slice-level quarantine that alone could make such a descriptor safe, and several downstream predicates still compare that field with the cross-source comparator.  A zero-epoch recovery therefore runs (replay, purge, slot zeroing) under an incarnation it cannot name, cannot be taken over or fence-certified if its owner dies mid-flight, and defeats the P237-SLOT-REOCCUPIED dedup that exists to stop a live successor being re-fenced.
defects.evidence: CODE-VERIFIED sess91, with the reachability MEASURED rather than assumed — and the measurement corrected an over-claim made earlier in the same session.  TWO PRODUCERS of a zero victim_epoch. (1) The LEASE detector.  dlm/v5_mount.c:1405-1432 documents that v5_handle_node_death is reached from two detectors and that the lease layer 'only knows a node id stopped renewing and passes (-1, 0)', deliberately, 'to take the P237-RECOV-INC-UNOBSERVED arm'.  MEASURED on the fleet across every retained dmesg and journalctl -k: ZERO occurrences of a 'lease expired/died' line with slot -1 — this arm has never fired on this rig.  Why: the disklock monitor declares dead after DEAD_THRESHOLD(31) x HB_INTERVAL_MS(2000) = 62s plus a confirm sweep, while the lease timeout is MXFS_LEASE_TIMEOUT_DEFAULT_MS = 600000ms (dlm/lease.c:333).  The monitor always wins by ~5x.  NOTE, and this is a defect in its own right: the module parameter NAMED lease_timeout_ms does NOT set the lease timeout.  ctx->lease_timeout_ms is passed only to mxfs_disklock_set_dead_timeout_ms (v5_mount.c:2637, :2860), which converts it to disklock samples; nothing overrides lease.c:333.  So an operator tuning death detection by that knob shortens only the disk monitor, and the lease stays pinned at 10 minutes.  Net: the lease arm is reachable only when the disk monitor cannot witness a death for 600s — an unreadable HB sector, a wedged monitor thread, or a deployment where the disklock monitor is not the detector.  Real, but rare; NOT 'every node death' as this entry first claimed. (2) The MONITOR's own downgrade of a known incarnation to 0 — filed separately as D-MONITOR-INCARNATION-DOWNGRADE-TO-ZERO.  This is the producer actually exercised on the rig: sess91 drove it with tests/incarnation_mismatch_probe.sh arm=zero and observed the resulting descriptor published and completed at 0.11.421 ('P234-RECOV-FENCED slot=8 victim=4267470212 epoch=0 slice=0/4 owner=1638140017 gen=1 term=1' -> P163-RECOVERY-COMPLETE -> P97-SWEEP-DONE, slot zeroed, 0 NOTOURS / 0 REARMED).  On 0.11.420 the same descriptor could never be advanced at all (D-RECOV-AUTH-ZERO-VICTIM-EPOCH-WEDGE). REMAINING CROSS-SOURCE SITES, line-verified against 0.11.421 dlm/disklock.c: :414 recov_desc_names_inc (a zero-epoch descriptor can never be named by the incarnation-scoped API); :1194 disklock_hb_fn, the P237-SLOT-REOCCUPIED dedup, where a zero pending_epoch makes inc_eq(pending_epoch, victim_epoch) false so the death is RE-DECLARED — and the comment at that site states re-declaring 'would re-enter the expire path, whose FIRST act is a per-NODE fence — and the node is live again as the successor', i.e. a SAFETY consequence, not just liveness; :3416 mxfs_recov_cert_proves_exclusion (a zero epoch can never certify an incarnation fence); :3531 recovery_fence_intent and :3952 recovery_claim (both refuse unconditionally, so TAKEOVER of a zero-epoch recovery is impossible if its owner dies mid-flight — the same permanent-refusal class as the fixed wedge, through a different door).  MEASURED NOT a suspect: :2589 mxfs_disklock_clear_recovery_pending is ALREADY guarded — 'inc_valid(victim_epoch) && inc_valid(hade) && !inc_eq(...)' — and both probe arms confirmed it (P237-COMPLETE-REARMED=0, P237-PENDING-REARMED=0).  That guard does mean the sess86 COMPARE-and-clear silently degrades to a NODE-scoped clear whenever either incarnation is unknown, so a zero-epoch completion can retire a marker re-armed for a successor of the same node — the very hazard the compare-and-clear exists to prevent.
defects.mechanism: The design admits two incompatible readings of victim_epoch == 0: 'the incarnation is UNKNOWN' (what recovery_begin records) and 'no incarnation is being asserted' (what inc_eq refuses).  A descriptor that cannot name its victim incarnation cannot derive authority from incarnation identity; its authority would have to come from SLOT/slice-level quarantine.  The sess91 RULE-5 ruling lists what that requires and none of it is presently established: the guard must be acquired atomically with respect to slot admission; a new mount/incarnation must check the guard before using the slot; the victim's existing authority must be fenced by a mechanism that does not depend on knowing its epoch; replay and purge must be scoped to the frozen slot/descriptor rather than to victim_node; takeover must work by durable descriptor identity; clearing the guard must not race a new occupant; and a nonzero incarnation appearing while an unknown recovery is active needs a defined supersession action rather than treating 0 as matching it.
defects.containment: None.  0.11.421 makes the descriptor advanceable by its owner, which fixes the observed hang but does not establish that a recovery run under an unknown victim incarnation is SAFE.
defects.next: 1) THE CLOSURE STEP: a test that exercises the cause.  Inject epoch 0 into a victim's ACTIVE heartbeat record on the backing store, kill it, and assert P238-FENCE-ZEROINC fires and NO descriptor is laid on that slot.  Note the trap: the HB feature block's crc (hb_feature_crc) covers fs_gen/node_id/EPOCH, so a naive epoch rewrite makes hb_feature_state read !OK and a DIFFERENT arm fires — the injection must reseal the feature crc or the probe measures the wrong refusal.  tests/recov_takeover_doublefault_probe.sh has the host-side O_DIRECT read/write machinery and the offsets.  2) Items 1-2 of the original next list remain as HARDENING against recurrence rather than as live exposure: the provenance audit of each remaining comparison site, and the type split (an observed-incarnation type that cannot hold 0, versus a recovery-token type carrying a durable recovery_id plus a recorded_victim_epoch that may be 0).  Worth doing, but they now guard a class that cannot be constructed.
defects.found: sess91
defects.why_still_open:
SUBSTANTIALLY FIXED sess93 (0.11.426), NOT YET VERIFIED BY A TEST THAT EXERCISES THE CAUSE — which is why this is still OPEN rather than closed.

The sess91 RULE-5 ruling's item 3 offered a choice: prove seven quarantine invariants and keep zero-epoch descriptors, or FORBID THEM AT CREATION.  0.11.426 takes the second, and the class is now unconstructible rather than merely unlikely.  AUDIT, exhaustive: there are exactly TWO writers of desc.victim_epoch in the tree (grep 'recov.desc.victim_epoch\s*=' over dlm/) — disklock.c:2946 inside recovery_begin(), which is RETIRED and refuses at entry with P238-RECOV-BEGIN-RETIRED / -EPROTO; and disklock.c:3616 inside fence_intent(), which now refuses with P238-FENCE-ZEROINC / -EPROTO when the victim's own record carries !inc_valid(cur->epoch).  Upstream of both, v5_pr_fence_prove() refuses dead_epoch == 0 outright (P238-FENCE-NOINC / -ENODATA), so a lease-only detection — the only source of a zero — never reaches a creator at all.  Downstream, mxfs_recov_cert_proves_exclusion() has always required d->victim_epoch != 0, so even a zero-epoch descriptor written by an older build is refused by every gate.

ITEM 0 IS DONE (0.11.426).  The lease_timeout_ms module parameter was confirmed to configure ONLY mxfs_disklock_set_dead_timeout_ms — the lease's own timeout is MXFS_LEASE_TIMEOUT_DEFAULT_MS (600000, lease.h) and nothing ever writes it.  An operator setting lease_timeout_ms=15000 expecting a 15 s lease got a 15 s DISKLOCK threshold and a still-10-minute lease.  Renamed to dead_timeout_ms, with lease_timeout_ms kept as a working deprecated alias (dead_timeout_ms wins if both are set) that logs the correction at load.  The deliberate decision the entry asked for: the lease does NOT track it, per sess43 — a node that dies and rejoins takes a new node_id, so peers keep the dead identity ACTIVE in their lease table for up to ten minutes, and shortening that to match the disklock threshold would make a rejoining node race its own ghost.  RIG-VERIFIED: with MXFS_EXTRA_MODARGS='lease_timeout_ms=16000', test1 reports dead_timeout_ms=16000 resolved from the alias plus 'mxfs: lease_timeout_ms=16000 is DEPRECATED and has never configured the lease — it is the disklock dead-detection threshold.  Use dead_timeout_ms.  The lease timeout stays 600000 ms by design (sess43).'

ITEM 1's purge hazard is NOT PRESENT in the shipped signature: the ruling warned that the purge freeze gate must never accept a naked 'purge node N, epoch E' with E=0, but mxfs_disklock_purge_node(ctx, node_id) takes NO epoch argument — its freeze gate keys off the descriptor's own stage and owner_epoch.  And purge-by-node-id cannot hit a reincarnation because node ids are random per mount (MEASURED sess89), so a returning node never reuses its predecessor's id.

defects.summary: An abandoned recovery can NEVER be taken over: mxfs_disklock_recovery_takeover() has ZERO call sites in the entire tree.  If the elected replayer dies after publishing the durable recovery descriptor, every other survivor defers to it for ever ('another survivor owns this recovery; not publishing'), the victim's slot stays in RECOVERY_GUARD, its CAW grants stay frozen, and the slice is never replayed to completion.  Four further recovery-lifecycle entry points are equally unreachable, which also makes the entire sess74/75/76 fence-certificate lifecycle dead code.
defects.evidence: PROVEN BY EXHAUSTIVE GREP over every .c and .h in the tree, sess91 at 0.11.421.  Of the seven recovery-descriptor entry points, only TWO are wired: mxfs_disklock_recovery_begin (1 caller, dlm/v5_mount.c:2201) and mxfs_disklock_recovery_advance (2 callers, v5_mount.c:2254 and :2301).  The other five have NO callers at all — every occurrence is the definition itself or a prose mention in a comment: mxfs_disklock_recovery_takeover (dlm/disklock.c:3167 definition; :4908 a comment asserting 'abandoned recovery is resumed via mxfs_disklock_recovery_takeover()'), mxfs_disklock_recovery_claim (:3915), mxfs_disklock_recovery_fence_intent (:3486), mxfs_disklock_recovery_fence_certify (:3645 definition, :3009 a comment), and mxfs_disklock_recovery_fence_takeover (:3787).  MEASURED sess91 on the live 32-node rig at 0.11.421 with tests/recov_takeover_retry_probe.sh: kill test32 (slot 14), wait for a survivor to publish the descriptor (GUARD at t+63.4s, stage=3, owner_node=3454184023), then rewrite ONLY desc.owner_node to a value no live node holds and reseal the descriptor CRC.  The real owner then refused exactly ONCE — 'P234-RECOV-NOTOURS slot=14 victim=823118425 stage->5 kind=TAKEOVER (descriptor owner is not us)' — and stopped.  Every survivor thereafter logged 'P234-RECOV-OWNED slot=14 victim=823118425 owner=2545479693 gen=1 stage=3 — another survivor owns this recovery; not publishing' (x4 and counting).  Nobody owns it: the owner is a phantom.  P163-RECOVERY-COMPLETE=0 for the whole 133s observation window, the slot stayed in RECOVERY_GUARD at stage=3, and the victim's CAW grants stayed frozen behind the freeze gate.
defects.mechanism: MXFS_RECOV_ABANDON_MS (dlm/disklock.h:446) is 6000ms and the takeover CAS is fully implemented — abandonment is correctly defined as ABSENCE OF CHANGE in owner_stamp_ms across that window rather than by comparing clocks — but nothing ever calls the function that evaluates it, so the timeout is never consulted.  recovery_begin's own re-entry path returns -EBUSY with P234-RECOV-OWNED whenever the descriptor names another owner (disklock.c:2779-2785), which is correct in isolation and becomes a permanent deadlock precisely because no takeover exists to resolve it.  The freeze gate in mxfs_disklock_purge_node then refuses to zero a sector below GRANTS_RELEASED, so the slot and the dead victim's authority bits are held indefinitely.
defects.containment: None.  The survivors' log lines are individually correct and reassuring — each one truthfully says another node owns the recovery — so the deadlock is invisible without correlating all survivors and noticing that the named owner is not alive.
defects.next: CLOSED sess93.  Two residual items are tracked elsewhere rather than held here: (a) the FENCE-attempt takeover arm (recovery_fence_takeover, for a prover that dies holding the intent) is wired in the same function but has not been exercised — it is part of D-FENCE-CRASH-MATRIX-UNTESTED, which also covers the known-unrecoverable case where the prover dies AFTER a successful PREEMPT AND ABORT but before the certificate is durable; (b) GPT sess93 correction 2 requires proving foreign replay is safe to REPEAT after an owner died mid-write.  This run demonstrates one such resume (stage=3, replay already done, so the successor re-ran nothing), but the general case belongs to the crash matrix.
defects.found: sess91
defects.why_still_open: PARTIALLY FIXED, NOT YET VERIFIED (sess93, 0.11.422).  The unreachability is gone: mxfs_v5_dlm_recovery_acquire() (dlm/v5_mount.c) now calls mxfs_disklock_recovery_takeover() when recovery_claim returns -EBUSY AND the descriptor's owner_node is in this node's proved-dead set — which is exactly takeover's documented precondition, because v5_note_dead_node() is set only on the far side of a completed fence.  It also calls mxfs_disklock_recovery_fence_takeover() when the claim returns -EPERM and the descriptor is at stage FENCING with a PROVED-DEAD prover, then re-runs v5_pr_fence_prove() to issue a NEW PREEMPT AND ABORT and certify THAT result (never the dead prover's — sess74 ruled that inference unsound).  Both run on the foreign-replay workqueue / mount thread, never the heartbeat monitor, because takeover sleeps MXFS_RECOV_ABANDON_MS inside the call.  Elapsed time is never used as a proof of death.  BUT: neither arm has fired on the rig.  The sess93 fence-evidence probe run took the ordinary single-fault path (claim succeeded first try), so under RULE 6 this entry stays OPEN until a run EXERCISES the cause — the elected replayer dying mid-recovery — and shows P238-RECOV-TAKEOVER followed by P238-RECOV-TAKEN and a published recovery.
defects.disposition: FIXED AND VERIFIED sess93 (0.11.422).  CAUSE (RULE 4, proven sess91): mxfs_disklock_recovery_takeover() had ZERO callers.  The CAS was fully implemented, MXFS_RECOV_ABANDON_MS was defined, and a comment at disklock.c:4908 even asserted 'abandoned recovery is resumed via mxfs_disklock_recovery_takeover()' — describing a mechanism that never ran, so an elected replayer dying mid-recovery wedged the slice forever with the victim's CAW grants frozen behind it.  PATCH: mxfs_v5_dlm_recovery_acquire() (dlm/v5_mount.c) calls it when recovery_claim returns -EBUSY and the descriptor's owner_node is in this node's PROVED-DEAD set — which is precisely takeover's documented precondition, since v5_note_dead_node() is set only on the far side of a completed fence.  Elapsed time is never used as a death proof; the ABANDON_MS wait inside takeover re-proves only that nothing changed on the sector meanwhile.  It runs on the foreign-replay workqueue / mount thread, never the heartbeat monitor, because the call sleeps.  VERIFICATION that exercises the cause — a REAL DOUBLE FAULT, both deaths genuine hard kills, on the live 32-node CAW rig at 0.11.422 via the new tests/recov_takeover_doublefault_probe.sh: destroy victim test32 (slot 3, node 3629992608); a host-side O_DIRECT poll of the SCST backing store saw the RECOVERY_GUARD at t+62.8s and test1 (node 4143148027) claim the execution lease at t+64.6s; destroy test1 inside the ~8 s before it publishes.  test5 then logged, unprompted: 'P238-RECOV-TAKEOVER slot=3 node=3629992608 owner=4143148027 stage=3 — the elected replayer died mid-recovery and we proved it dead; attempting takeover', then 'P238-RECOV-TAKEN slot=3 node=3629992608 stage=3 — recovery taken over from a dead owner; RESUME from this stage, do not re-run earlier ones', then 'P163-RECOVERY-COMPLETE slot=3 node=3629992608' 15 s after the attempt began.  stage=3 is MXFS_RECOV_STAGE_IMAGES_REPLAYED, so test1 HAD replayed the slice and died before publishing, and test5 correctly resumed from that milestone instead of re-running it.  UNGATED completes=0 throughout.  Before 0.11.422 that slice wedged permanently — sess91 measured exactly that outcome (P163-RECOVERY-COMPLETE=0 for the whole window, slot frozen at stage=3).  Board context: the full 32/caw board on the same build is 25 PASS / 0 FAIL under unchanged acceptance criteria.

defects.summary: When exclusion cannot be proved, MXFS correctly refuses to replay a dead peer's journal slice — but the resulting blocked recovery is visible ONLY as kernel log lines (P238-FENCE-UNPROVEN / -NOPR / -UNRECORDED / -COMPLETE-UNFENCED, P236-CLAIM-UNCERTIFIED).  There is no durable, queryable state, so a filesystem whose peers are stalled on a frozen victim's grants is indistinguishable from one that is simply hung, and an operator has nothing to act on.
defects.found: RULE-5 GPT ruling, sess93 (banked in ccmemory as ccloop-c7ee71c6-sess93-GPT-ruling-fence-evidence-wiring).  Raised while ruling on how to wire the fence-evidence channel; the ruling states the release unit is seven things, of which 0.11.422 landed the first four.
evidence: GPT sess93 Q2: 'Add an explicit durable and observable state, not merely repeated log lines... Mount status should clearly say that the filesystem is blocked on unproven exclusion, rather than appearing hung.'
0.11.422 dlm/v5_mount.c v5_pr_fence_prove() returns >0 for every non-proving outcome and logs; nothing records it anywhere a tool can read.

0.11.422 mxfs_v5_dlm_recovery_acquire() returns -EPERM as an unbounded WAIT state by design (there is deliberately no timeout after which replay becomes allowed), so the blocked condition can persist indefinitely with no surfaced status.

MEASURED sess93 (tests/excl_lapse_probe.sh, 0.11.424): a slice whose exclusion lapsed retried indefinitely — P238-RECOV-LEASE -> P239-EXCL-RETURNED -> P239-EXCL-LAPSED at t=1061.3, 1091.5 and 1121.7 s and continuing, i.e. every ~30 s (the freplay re-arm period), with the slice's grants frozen the whole time and NOTHING outside dmesg recording that the filesystem was blocked.  The refusal is correct; the absence of a surfaced state is the defect.  Note each retry re-claims the execution lease before re-checking, so the loop also churns the descriptor's owner fields.
defects.mechanism: The gate is correct and the refusal is deliberate; what is missing is the reporting surface.  Required fields per the ruling: victim node/slot/epoch, victim key, prover node/epoch, fence term, last SCSI result and a normalised reason, observed reservation type and PR generation, first-failure and last-attempt timestamps, retry count, whether the owner is live, which locks/slice are blocked, and the permitted administrative actions.
defects.next: CLOSED sess93.  Follow-ups that are NOT this entry: (a) the file is per-mount debugfs, so a cluster-wide view still means visiting each node — acceptable for now, and a cluster-aggregating tool belongs with the other tools/ work rather than in the kernel; (b) 'mount status should clearly say it is blocked' is satisfied by an explicit queryable file but not by anything statfs/df would show — if that is wanted it should be filed as its own item with a decision about which syscall surface carries it.
defects.disposition: FIXED AND VERIFIED sess93 (0.11.425).  CAUSE: every refusal the fence-evidence work added fails CLOSED, and a fail-closed recovery is indistinguishable from a hang from outside — peers block on the frozen victim's locks either way.  MEASURED (tests/excl_lapse_probe.sh on 0.11.424): a slice whose exclusion had lapsed retried every ~30 s indefinitely with the entire story visible only in dmesg.  PATCH: a per-victim-slot RECOVERY_BLOCKED_FENCE record (struct mxfs_recov_blocked, dlm/v5_mount.h) set at every refusal point in v5_pr_fence_prove(), v5_exclusion_recheck() and mxfs_v5_dlm_recovery_acquire(), cleared only when the recovery actually publishes, and exposed at /sys/kernel/debug/mxfs/<dev>/recovery_blocked.  Ten named reasons (NO_PR, FENCE_UNPROVEN, CERT_UNRECORDED, NO_INTENT, NO_CERTIFICATE, OWNED_ELSEWHERE, EXCL_LAPSED, SELF_FENCED, NO_INCARNATION).  The kernel-API half lives in xfs/xfs_mxfs_dlm.c, not dlm/, so the DLM layer still builds user-mode (architectural invariant 4); dlm/ exposes only mxfs_v5_dlm_blocked_iter() filling a caller-provided struct.  first_ms is stamped once and KEPT — how long a slice has been unrecoverable is the number an operator acts on, and restamping it per retry would hide exactly that.  VERIFICATION on the live 32-node CAW rig: healthy cluster -> the file exists and is EMPTY.  After tests/excl_lapse_probe.sh made a fenced victim 'return' (slot 3, node 3772707794), test1's file read: 'RECOVERY_BLOCKED_FENCE - these journal slices cannot be recovered... This is a REFUSAL, not a hang' followed by 'slot=3 reason=EXCL_LAPSED rc=-1 / victim node=3772707794 incarnation=11921365376053614700 key=0xe0def3d2 / fence kind=KEY_ABSENT_UNPROVEN(6) resv_type=0x05 pr_gen=3068 term=0 / ownership prover=0 recovery_owner=0 / timing blocked_for_ms=92822 attempts=4 last_attempt_ms_ago=2243' and the matching ACTION text ('the fenced victim is REGISTERED AGAIN and can write to this LUN right now.  Stop it, or fence it at the target').  Every field the ledger entry demanded is present.  The probe now ASSERTS the surface is non-empty, so a regression that silently drops it fails the probe.  Board: full 32/caw on 0.11.425 is 26 PASS / 0 FAIL under unchanged acceptance criteria.

defects.summary: A clustered read-write mount is admitted without ever checking that its configured fencing mechanism can actually produce the evidence recovery will require.  The first time anyone discovers that PR is absent, the reservation is not WR_EX_RO, the key view is truncated, or the topology is advisory, is AFTER a peer has died — at which point the slice is unrecoverable and peers are already blocked on its grants.
defects.found: RULE-5 GPT ruling, sess93 (banked in ccmemory as ccloop-c7ee71c6-sess93-GPT-ruling-fence-evidence-wiring).  Raised while ruling on how to wire the fence-evidence channel; the ruling states the release unit is seven things, of which 0.11.422 landed the first four.
evidence: GPT sess93 Q2: 'discovering this only after a node dies is also not release-grade.  A clustered read-write mount should validate, before admitting normal I/O, that its configured fencing mechanism can actually produce the required evidence.'

dlm/scsipr.c mxfs_scsipr_fence_node() can return NO_RESERVATION, ADVISORY_TOPOLOGY, UNSUPPORTED, NOT_REGISTERED or VIEW_TRUNCATED — each of which makes every future recovery on that mount impossible — and none of them is tested at mount.
0.11.422 dlm/v5_mount.c logs P238-FENCE-NOPR only on the death path, i.e. exactly too late.

sess93: PERSISTENT RESERVE IN / REPORT CAPABILITIES is the readable source for most of what this check needs and MXFS never issues it.  On the rig it returns PTPL_C=1, PTPL_A=1, CRH=1, SIP_C=1, ATP_C=1, TMV=1 and a type mask listing WE-RO — i.e. capability, persistence state, and supported reservation types are all available in ONE command at mount time.  (This is also where D-PR-REGISTRATION-NOT-PERSISTENT-APTPL's surviving half landed when that entry was DISPROVED: the APTPL bit IS set by sd_pr_register, but nothing verifies PTPL_A is actually active, and on a target that does not persist PR state the whole cross-boot recovery story changes silently.)
defects.mechanism: Admission must verify: PR available; reservation held and exactly WR_EX_RO; every admitted writer registered; PR view complete (not truncated); topology not advisory; required persistence present.  A rig that cannot satisfy this must be explicitly single-node, read-only, or given another fencing provider — never silently given weaker production semantics, which is what happens today.
defects.next: 1) Add the admission check to the mount path, before normal I/O is admitted: issue PERSISTENT RESERVE IN / REPORT CAPABILITIES (assert PTPL_A=1 and that the type mask offers WE-RO), READ RESERVATION (held, type WR_EX_RO), and READ KEYS (view NOT truncated, our own key present).  mxfs_scsipr_exclusion_holds() already implements the last two — factor the shared part rather than duplicating it.  2) Decide and document the failure action per condition (refuse the mount / mount read-only / mount single-node); GPT sess93 Q2 requires that a rig which cannot produce fencing evidence be explicitly one of those and never silently given weaker production semantics.  3) Criterion: mount against a target with no reservation held and assert the mount does not silently come up read-write.

defects.summary: MXFS does not request APTPL (Activate Persist Through Power Loss) on its PR registrations or reservation, so a target restart silently drops all PR state.  Every stale slot's victim key then reads ABSENT, which is correctly non-proving, so under the 0.11.422 gate NO mount can ever recover those slices: a routine storage restart makes the filesystem operationally unrecoverable with frozen grants.
defects.found: RULE-5 GPT ruling, sess93 (banked in ccmemory as ccloop-c7ee71c6-sess93-GPT-ruling-fence-evidence-wiring).  Raised while ruling on how to wire the fence-evidence channel; the ruling states the release unit is seven things, of which 0.11.422 landed the first four.
evidence: GPT sess93 Q4: 'PR registrations vanishing after a target restart may mean only that the target lost volatile PR state.  Therefore KEY_ABSENT_UNPROVEN must remain non-proving... MXFS should request AND VERIFY APTPL.'
dlm/scsipr.c — no APTPL bit is set on REGISTER_AND_IGNORE or RESERVE, and nothing verifies persistence.

dlm/disklock.c mxfs_recov_cert_proves_exclusion() requires fence_kind PREEMPT_ABORT_DONE, which mxfs_scsipr_fence_node can only produce when the victim key is PRESENT (scsipr.c:441 returns KEY_ABSENT_UNPROVEN otherwise) — so a post-restart cohort is permanently uncertifiable.
defects.mechanism: Setting the bit is not enough: the ruling requires verifying that registrations and the reservation are genuinely persistent and that the reservation stays WR_EX_RO, and rejecting clustered RW operation (or requiring another fencing provider) when persistence is unavailable.  It also needs a stale-persistent-key cleanup policy, because node ids are random per mount (measured sess89) so keys would otherwise accumulate without bound — cleanup tied to proved-dead incarnations only, never removing current members.
defects.next: CLOSED sess93 as DISPROVED.  Two things the entry raised are real and are tracked where they belong, NOT dropped: (1) 'request AND VERIFY' — MXFS still never checks at mount that persistence is actually in force, which is D-FENCE-CAPABILITY-UNVALIDATED-AT-MOUNT's admission check (now explicitly required to read REPORT CAPABILITIES and assert PTPL_A).  (2) stale-key accumulation from random per-mount ids — NOT observed: the rig carries 62-64 key descriptors for 32 nodes, i.e. exactly 2 per node for the two multipath paths, with no residue from earlier incarnations.  If a future measurement shows accumulation, file it fresh rather than reopening this.  METHOD LESSON, recorded because it cost a filing: a grep of MXFS's source is NOT sufficient evidence about SCSI-level behaviour.  MXFS delegates PR to the kernel block PR API, so what actually reaches the wire is decided in drivers/scsi/sd.c.  Check the target's REPORT CAPABILITIES before asserting anything about what MXFS does or does not request.
defects.disposition: DISPROVED sess93, same session it was filed, on direct evidence.  THE CLAIM WAS WRONG: I filed it after grepping MXFS's own source for 'aptpl' and finding nothing.  The bit is set ONE LAYER DOWN, outside that grep's reach.  MXFS registers through the Linux block PR API (pal/linux/kern.c: ops->pr_register(bdev, 0, key, PR_FL_IGNORE_KEY)), and /src/linux drivers/scsi/sd.c sd_pr_register() ends with `sd_pr_out_command(bdev, 0x06, old_key, new_key, 0, (1 << 0) /* APTPL */)` — the APTPL bit is set UNCONDITIONALLY on every REGISTER AND IGNORE EXISTING KEY, landing in byte 20 of the PROUT parameter list.  RIG CORROBORATION, three independent observations: (a) PERSISTENT RESERVE IN / REPORT CAPABILITIES on the live LUN returns 'Persist Through Power Loss Capable(PTPL_C): 1' AND 'Persist Through Power Loss Active(PTPL_A): 1' — the target says persistence is not merely supported but ACTIVE, which only a registration carrying APTPL=1 can do; (b) the SCST device exports pr_file_name=/var/lib/scst/pr/mxfs and that file exists (4820 bytes, current timestamp) holding the full registrant table; (c) /sys/kernel/scst_tgt/devices/mxfs/pr_state shows every registrant recorded against a STABLE transport identity — the initiator's iSCSI IQN, e.g. 'iqn.2004-10.com.ubuntu:01:test1-mxfs-node,i,0x200003d0200' — not just the random per-mount key.  So PR state on this stack survives a target restart, and the impact I asserted ('a routine storage restart makes the filesystem operationally unrecoverable') does not occur.  NOTE for completeness: sd_pr_reserve/preempt/clear/release all send APTPL=0, which is correct — SPC-4 gives the bit meaning only in REGISTER and REGISTER AND IGNORE EXISTING KEY, and PTPL_A stays active once a registration sets it.

defects.summary: CONFIRMED BY DIRECT MEASUREMENT (sess93).  A PREEMPT AND ABORT excludes the victim only at the INSTANT it completes.  Seconds later the same node re-registers with a fresh key and writes to the shared LUN — so for the entire duration of the foreign-slice replay that the fence certificate authorises, the only thing keeping a partitioned victim off the shared metadata is that victim's OWN cooperative self-fence.
defects.found: MEASURED sess93 on the live 32-node CAW rig at the SCSI layer, bypassing MXFS entirely: tests/pr_reregister_probe.sh (victim test32 key=0x37e3d796, preemptor test1 key=0x434d2436, WE-RO reservation held by 0x434d2436, scratch LBA 131087).
evidence: STEP 1 baseline — victim writes LBA 131087 with 0xa5: rc=0, post-read matches.  The victim can write before the fence, so the rest of the probe is meaningful.

STEP 2 — test1 issues sg_persist --out --preempt-abort --param-rk=0x434d2436 --param-sark=0x37e3d796 --prout-type=5: rc=0, and READ KEYS then shows 0 descriptors matching 0x37e3d796.  The victim's registration is gone.

STEP 3 — victim writes LBA 131087 with 0x5a: rc=1, and the pre-read still shows a5 a5 a5...  REFUSED.  Exclusion genuinely works at that instant, which is what the certificate claims and all it claims.

STEP 4a — victim issues sg_persist --out --register-ignore --param-sark=0xfeed0001: rc=0.  THE TARGET ACCEPTED THE RE-REGISTRATION.  Nothing in SPC forbids REGISTER_AND_IGNORE from an unregistered initiator, and the WE-RO reservation does not prevent it.
STEP 4b — victim writes LBA 131087 with 0x33: rc=0, post-read '33 33 33 33 33 33 33 33'.  THE WRITE LANDED.  A node the cluster had just fenced put bytes on the shared LUN.

dlm/scsipr.c — MXFS's only defence is cooperative: mxfs_scsipr_self_check notices the key is gone and the node force-shuts-down (MXFS_FENCE_KIND_SELF_PREEMPTED / P131-SELF-FENCE, explicitly 'no auto-re-register').  That requires the victim's kernel to still be running and still scheduling — precisely what is in doubt about a node just declared dead by 62 s of missed heartbeats.

GPT RULE-5 ruling sess93, requirement B, which prompted the measurement: 'If a partitioned old node can simply register its key again, the certificate is only historical evidence and is not enough to protect replay.'
defects.mechanism: The certificate records a true fact with a SHELF LIFE, and nothing enforces the interval it is consumed over.  The window that matters is [certificate durable .. recovery published] — on the rig that is roughly 8 s of foreign log replay writing shared XFS metadata in place.  A victim that is alive but partitioned (CPU-starved, network-isolated, or simply slow enough to miss 31 heartbeat samples) is not obliged to notice anything: it re-registers on its next I/O retry and resumes writing into the same metadata the replayer is rebuilding. Acceptable enforcement per the ruling must sit BELOW ordinary filesystem writes: target ACL revocation for the victim's initiator, fabric/session revocation, or a membership protocol that blocks re-registration until recovery completes.  Making the self-fence faster or more reliable does NOT close it — any cooperative mechanism assumes the victim is healthy enough to cooperate, which is the assumption the fence exists to drop.

defects.why_it_was_not_caught: Every criterion that exercises fencing kills the victim with 'virsh destroy', which is a power cut: the victim is not merely fenced, it is GONE, so it never attempts anything afterwards.  The dangerous case — a victim that is fenced and still running — has never been produced by any test.  This probe produces it by preempting a HEALTHY node's key.
fix: DESIGN RULED (GPT RULE-5, sess93 follow-up; full text in ccmemory ccloop-c7ee71c6-sess93-GPT-ruling-2-fence-enforcement-options).  The headline is that the measurement 'invalidates PREEMPT AND ABORT as a durable host fence' and that for an ordinary shared-write SCSI LUN there is NO fully sound, persistent, in-band fence against a still-running initiator that may register under a fresh key: SCSI PR does not bind keys to cluster identity, does not authorize who may register, and provides no deny-list.

RANKED OPTIONS.  (1) TARGET/FABRIC REVOCATION is the sound general answer — revoke every path for the victim's STABLE initiator identity (IQN/WWPN/host object/ACL), covering all sessions, aborting or draining outstanding commands, rejecting both ordinary I/O AND PR OUT, remaining in force until explicit readmission, surviving recovery-owner failure.  It is necessarily outside a portable kernel filesystem module: it needs a fencing agent, an array API, a cluster fencing daemon, or an administrator.  (2) TEMPORARY WRITE EXCLUSIVE is the best purely in-band option and is CONDITIONALLY sound for the replay window only.  (3) The re-check now shipped in 0.11.424 is detect-only.  (4) Periodic PREEMPT AND ABORT is UNSOUND — it targets the ORIGINAL key and a returning victim picks a new one, and 'bounded exposure time is not bounded damage: one accepted sector write invalidates the recovery'.  Enumerate-and-preempt-unknown-keys is ALSO UNSOUND — the read/classify/preempt sequence is inherently non-atomic and it makes the recoverer an unauthenticated target membership authority.

THE TEMPORARY-WE DESIGN, if taken: convert WE-RO to ordinary single-holder WRITE EXCLUSIVE for the replay window so the TARGET rejects writes from every non-holder including a victim that successfully re-registers.  Six binding requirements: (a) quiesce ALL cooperating nodes first — stop new writes and drain outstanding I/O on every healthy node, because RESERVATION CONFLICT escaping into XFS shuts filesystems down ('convert and let their I/O bounce' is unsound); (b) no unreserved gap — never RELEASE-then-RESERVE, use an atomic PR transition and verify the exact SPC behaviour on BOTH LIO and SCST and on representative arrays; (c) still issue PREEMPT AND ABORT, because WE stops only LATER non-holder writes while commands already outstanding at the victim's nexus must be aborted, and the gate certificate is issued only after that boundary; (d) hold WE continuously through replay and publication; (e) takeover must ATOMICALLY acquire or transfer the single-writer reservation, with no unreserved or WE-RO interval; (f) restore WE-RO only after publication.  Healthy nodes keep their registrations (less churn); a non-holder registrant still cannot write.  Two stated limits: it protects only while held, so it is not a permanent host fence; and SCSI PR is not Byzantine-safe — an initiator able to issue PR OUT can read the reservation key and try to preempt the WE holder, so it is sound only under the narrower model that stale nodes resume data I/O and registration but do not steal the reservation.

THE CERTIFICATE MUST BE RENAMED.  GPT: 'Your existing certificate should no longer be called a fence certificate unless it represents either a continuing exclusive-write reservation or continuing target/fabric exclusion.  PREEMPT AND ABORT alone is evidence of a completed eviction event, not evidence that the host remains fenced.'  Under a WE gate it would read 'recovery epoch E currently owns the target-enforced exclusive write gate', not 'victim key K was absent at time T'.

AND THE FORMULATION THAT IS NOT AVAILABLE: in-place foreign XFS log replay has a quiet write domain as a HARD PRECONDITION.  'There is no credible small reformulation in which current in-place XFS replay remains correct while an arbitrary partitioned victim may concurrently write the same LUN.'  Tolerating a concurrent stale writer would need an architecture change: COW recovery into an isolated clone plus an atomic namespace/LUN switch, immutable epoch-separated metadata, target-enforced write capabilities, or a target-side compare-and-publish primitive.  On-disk epoch tags detect stale writes after the fact but cannot stop a stale initiator overwriting the sector holding the new data or tag.

2026-08-04 sess131 — MECHANISM CHOSEN (next_step item 1 DISCHARGED) + RULE-5 RULING. CODE FACT: the mechanism already exists in-tree and was simply never applied to the 0.11.422 change. Three-layer C7 gate: (1) XFS_SB_FEAT_INCOMPAT_MXFS_PROTOGATE bit 30 (xfs/libxfs/xfs_format.h:412), set by mkfs_mxfs, in XFS_SB_FEAT_INCOMPAT_ALL — pre-gate kernels inherit upstream's unknown-incompat refusal (one-shot, preventative only); (2) envelope MXFS_FORMAT_F_PROTOGATE + cluster_proto_gen, enforced == MXFS_PROTO_GEN at pal/linux/xfs_super.c:3014-3029 with -EPROTONOSUPPORT plus a half-upgraded-format check; (3) disklock HB feature block — P-VERGATE-JOIN (-EPROTO) join refusal and monitor P-VERGATE-FENCE (dlm/disklock.c:1289, 2509). MXFS_PROTO_GEN is 3 (include/mxfs/mxfs_super.h:90); it went 1->2 at sess75 for recovery-descriptor v2 and 2->3 at sess86 for the nonzero mount incarnation. THE 0.11.422 CERTIFIED-REPLAY GATE DID NOT BUMP IT, so a pre-0.11.422 / post-incarnation binary is gen 3, is admitted by all three layers, and performs exactly the ungated replay this entry describes. The sess74 ruling quoted at include/mxfs/mxfs_super.h:56-88 and dlm/disklock.h:293-304 applies verbatim: per-record fail-closed is no substitute because the old replayer REPLAYS FIRST and consults the descriptor only afterwards. RULE-5 RULING (sess131, gpt-5.6-sol; full text in ccmemory ccloop-c7ee71c6-sess131-GPT-ruling-protogen4-and-quarantine): MXFS_PROTO_GEN 3->4 is APPROVED and REQUIRED — the certified-replay rule is a cluster protocol generation change even though the descriptor encoding is byte-identical, because the set of permitted participants and writes changed. FOUR MANDATORY BLOCKERS before this entry may close: (B1) recovery must be unreachable until envelope admission — a gen-3 kernel could begin foreign replay before discovering the envelope says 4, and layer 3 cannot repair replay that already happened; require an immutable proto_admitted mount-state bit asserted at EVERY recovery entry point, and audit normal mount, remount/retry, partial-mount error recovery, deferred recovery workers, mount-time XFS journal recovery callbacks, snapshot/secondary-sb paths, and administrative recover-only entry points. (B2) 3->4 must be an OFFLINE CLUSTER TRANSITION, not an offline metadata write: an already-mounted or suspended gen-3 node does not reread the envelope and may resume and replay before the gen-4 monitor fences it — stop/unmount every member, take an exclusive maintenance/storage lease, revoke/preempt all old PR registrations, invalidate the old membership epoch, and keep suspended nodes off the LUN until remount. (B3) the generation update must be a crash-safe activation transaction: all authoritative envelope copies written with FUA/flush, an unambiguous interrupted-upgrade state, and readers FAIL CLOSED on disagreement rather than picking an older valid copy. (B4) gen 4 names a BEHAVIORAL CONTRACT — certified-replay check, descriptor-write restrictions and mount ordering are conformance requirements for any build claiming 4, with mixed-build tests proving every gen-3 build is rejected BEFORE recovery starts. ROLLOUT: 'accept N and N-1 read-only' is REJECTED as unsafe — a read-only mount may still perform journal recovery and foreign replay IS mount-time recovery. Hard refusal is the correct default. LIMITATION that must be written into the upgrade procedure: the bump is PROSPECTIVE; it does not prove no gen-3 node already performed an ungated replay, and the ABSENCE of a stale FENCED/NONE descriptor is not proof of safety because an unsafe replay may have completed and been purged. Finding legacy or suspicious recovery records must trigger scrub/fsck and an operator-visible 'previously exposed to ungated replay' status.

2026-08-04 sess131 — QUARANTINE DESIGN (next_step item 2) RULED UNSOUND AS PROPOSED. I proposed that any survivor durably set MXFS_RECOV_F_QUARANTINED (dlm/disklock.h:357) on a legacy uncertified FENCED/NONE descriptor, since today such a descriptor merely fails mxfs_recov_cert_proves_exclusion() with reason 'fence_kind does not prove exclusion' (dlm/disklock.c:3483) and blocks its slot forever with no operator-visible reason. REJECTED. (B5) 'one-way and strictly more restrictive' is NOT a substitute for write authority: a survivor can hold a stale sector image and race the victim's heartbeat update, a recovery owner advancing or replacing the descriptor, a purge or reuse for a NEW incarnation, another survivor becoming owner, or a sector-level read-modify-write over unrelated fields — overwriting newer state, quarantining a REUSED slot, or corrupting the CRC-protected sector. (B6) a survivor must not write the victim's sector before the victim is excluded; proven exclusion is required for ANY survivor-side descriptor mutation unless an independent atomic quarantine location exists that the victim never writes. Owner-only quarantine is acceptable ONLY with ownership acquired via the existing owner/epoch protocol, identity + incarnation + sequence + expected-old-contents revalidated at commit, the same durable/conditional serialization as other descriptor advances, and victim-sector write safety already established. OTHERWISE the correct runtime behavior is: refuse replay, leave the descriptor UNCHANGED, and publish a persistent health event / named rate-limited alert. (B7) no disposition or repair model exists yet for legacy obligations — an unmarked blocked descriptor is NOT equivalent to a quarantined one, because the unmarked one can still be repaired by future software while the terminal flag forbids it; choose ONE policy first: permanent abandonment, certified reconstruction (fresh certified exclusion, revalidate identity/incarnation and journal state AFTER exclusion, build a NEW recovery transaction, never bless the old NONE descriptor), or offline administrative discharge. DO NOT add a generic clear-quarantine operation. UPGRADER: chk_mxfs --upgrade-protogate should INVENTORY AND REPORT, not auto-quarantine — scan all descriptor locations and redundant copies, classify each, emit a durable report naming slot/victim identity/incarnation/stage/reason, and offer leave-unresolved-and-activate, an explicit destructive --quarantine-legacy, or a designed reconstruction. (B8) it must NEVER synthesize a fence certificate because the tool believes the cluster is offline; administrative offline status is not proof the victim was excluded at the relevant time. Explicitly REJECTED: refusing the whole generation upgrade whenever a NONE descriptor exists — leaving the volume at gen 3 preserves an old binary's ability to mount and replay ungated, which is strictly worse.

defects.found: Code/design proof, not yet exercised by a test. SHIPPED since sess48 (0.11.395), which introduced ex_grant_epoch.
defects.summary: The durable write-authority token ex_grant_epoch is documented and consumed as a uint64 that uniquely names one exclusive tenure, but it is assigned from the uint32 slot generation (dlm/dlm_caw.c:956, the single assignment site in the tree). It is therefore a zero-extended 32-bit CYCLIC token, not a unique identity: after 2^32 successful CASes on a slot the token REPEATS, and at the wrap point generation==0 mints the value the protocol defines as invalid. generation advances on EVERY successful CAS of the slot — waiter registration included, not just grants — so a hot resource reaches wrap far sooner than a count of exclusive tenures would suggest.
defects.mechanism: dlm/dlm_caw.c:956 caw_grant_epoch_update(): `s->ex_grant_epoch = s->generation;` with `uint32_t generation` and `uint64_t ex_grant_epoch`. Two distinct failures: (1) TOKEN REUSE — a crash-recovery replayer validating a logged image by epoch equality can match a record written under an EARLIER tenure that happened to carry the same post-wrap value, and accept a foreign image as authorized; (2) ZERO MINT — at the wrap the granting CAS stamps 0, which caw_grant_result_fill classifies as MXFS_GAUTH_WRITE_ZERO_EPOCH, i.e. the fail-closed 'slot was tombstoned and the namespace restarted' signal. A live, legitimately-granted EX tenure then reports itself as having no authority.
defects.evidence: grep -rn 'ex_grant_epoch *=' --include=*.c --include=*.h over the whole tree returns exactly ONE assignment, dlm/dlm_caw.c:956, inside caw_grant_epoch_update. Field declarations: dlm/dlm_caw.h:274 `uint64_t ex_grant_epoch` vs the slot's `uint32_t generation`. The uniqueness claim the consumers rely on is stated in the sess48 comment at dlm/dlm_caw.c:950-955 ('uniquely names this exclusive acquisition ... new on EVERY reacquire') and in include/mxfs/mxfs_dlm.h:96-121. RULE-5 ruling sess107 (ccmemory ccloop-c7ee71c6-sess107-GPT-ruling-direct-handoff-mint-10-blockers) ruled the current token unsound and the wrap/zero handling release-blocking.
defects.blast_radius: Every consumer of durable write authority: the per-inode install path (xfs/xfs_mxfs_dlm.c, mxfs_grant_result.grant_epoch), the AG token stamped lock-free into every buffer-log record via pag->pag_mxfs_grant_epoch, and the foreign-slice replay gate that D-FOREIGN-REPLAY-UNGATED-IMAGES exists to build. A reused token defeats the gate in the accept direction (false authority); a zero token defeats it in the refuse direction (a legitimate tenure reports none).
